newsitem.title: UK: U.S. rate rise expected but reality to hurt bonds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rate rise expected but reality to hurt bonds.

text.p: International bond markets are primed for a U.S. interest rate rise on Tuesday but analysts said the reality would hit hard.

Markets might hold up initially or even rally, but aftershocks would be painful as investors factored in not only rising rates in the United States but also increases to come in Europe and Japan, they said.

"A rate rise in the U.S. would be negative for global bond markets and would confirm we are heading for a change in the interest rate cycle this year," said Graham McDevitt, head of bond strategy at Paribas Capital Markets in London.
The U.S. central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on Tuesday to consider monetary policy. Bond markets and many economists are betting on a rise.
The odds on an increase shortened dramatically last Thursday after Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan stressed the importance of pre-emptive action to tame inflation.

A Reuter poll of 48 economists after Greenspan's remarks showed 34 expected the Fed to raise its federal funds target to at least 5.50 percent on Tuesday from 5.25 percent. In the same survey a week before only 17 out of 44 expected a rise.

The U.S. Treasury yield curve has also flattened significantly since Thursday, with the yield spread between the two-year note and the 30-year bond narrowing to 68 basis points from 77 at last Wednesday's close.
With a rate rise so well priced in, markets could in fact rally if the Fed did decide to raise rates, said George Magnus, chief international economist at UBS in London.
But any strength would be short-lived.

"One's really hard pressed to say a Fed rate hike is positive for global bonds," Magnus said. "It may be for a day or two but the fundamentals that are giving rise to this Fed rate hike are actually causing sentiment in Japan and Europe to turn."

Analysts said it would be hard for the yield on the long bond to stay around 7.0 percent even if a rise was accompanied by a statement stressing the move was only cautionary. Analysts pegged initial targets of 7.15 percent and 7.25 percent.
Magnus expected international debt markets to follow any downward move in the Treasury market closely, although rate rises in Japan and continental Europe were still some way off.

"If the European economy was still in a powerless condition there might be some reason to believe European bonds could tread water but there has been a marked shift in Europe's cyclical position and a fairly genuine business recovery," Magnus said.
McDevitt at Paribas, who expected a German rate rise later this year, said short-term German debt was vulnerable.

"The first reaction will be negative at the front end of the German yield curve, not that Germany is expecting a rate rise but it will be negative in terms of sentiment," he said. "And that is exactly what happened in 1994 when the Bundesbank was clearly cutting rates."
The Fed last raised interest rates in February 1994, sending bond markets into a bearish mode through much of the year.

McDevitt saw good support for 10-year Bunds at 6.0 percent, which corresponds to about 99.34 on June Bund futures, near strong technical support. "If Bunds break through those support levels that is going to be very negative," he said.
Analysts said how far markets would fall on a rate rise hinged on whether they expected another one to follow.
Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International here, thought markets would find their feet quickly.

"People will use any opportunity to buy at the lower levels," he said. "It will be an insurance tightening. I think all the Fed will be looking to do will be to take rates back to the peak of the cycle which was 6.00 percent."
Magnus was more pessimistic. Markets will be volatile and jittery as they await the Fed's next step.
"The one thing the statement cannot do is tell us whether this is a one-off move," he said.
